title: AI Proofreading AI校对
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing using artificial intelligence as a proofreading tool.
 
Speaker 1 (Boy A - Curious): Hey guys, I’ve been thinking about trying to use AI tools to look over my essay draft tonight. I really need something to check grammar for him and maybe provide him some ideas for the overall improvement of the assignment. But honestly, I'm not sure if it's okay under our university guidelines.
Speaker 2 (Girl B - Fear): Oh, definitely be careful with that. I won't risk using AI at all for my course submissions. I am deeply concerned with plagiarism issue cases popping up lately, and using automated text generators poses a significant risk to our academic standing. If the system flags it, we could get zero for the module.
Speaker 3 (Boy C - Tool): Hmm, I see your point, but I actually doesn't mind using AI as a basic editing assistant. To me, it's just like using standard computer software to check grammar, like spellcheck or Grammarly. You aren't trying to use others' words dishonestly; you're just using the tech to improve their own vocabulary and polish your linguistic expressions. I think it's worth a give a try.
Speaker 2 (Girl B - Fear): I don't know, it still feels like a slippery slope. What if it alters your phrasing so much that it's no longer your own work?
Speaker 1 (Boy A - Curious): Yeah, that's exactly why I'm hesitant. Maybe I should ask for advice from the tutor during office hours tomorrow. Getting some direct feedback from my tutor on what boundaries we need to follow would make me feel way safer. I think I'll just go back and ask my tutor before I copy-paste anything into those apps.
Speaker 3 (Boy C - Tool): That's a fair choice, but remember, the AI won't get any new ideas for you out of thin air anyway. It doesn't think for itself. Its main job is just to help make ideas clearer on the page. Plus, it's just a faster way to learn vocabulary from other sources while editing your own drafts.
Speaker 2 (Girl B - Fear): Well, I suppose if you're just fixing commas, I don't really think it would go that far as to be called cheating. But still, I’d rather just write everything entirely on my own to stay completely safe.
Speaker 3 (Boy C - Tool): Haha, well, it's entirely up to you. Everyone has their own study method.
Speaker 1 (Boy A - Curious): True. I'll check with the department tomorrow morning. If the tutor gives me the green light to use it strictly as a proofreader, I'll give it a shot. Otherwise, I'm sticking to the old-fashioned way!

instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.

Two girls and one boy talk about sports, keeping exercising and staying active outdoors.
 
Speaker 1 (Girl A - Nature): I have to admit, guys, I'm not a big fan of outdoor sports at all. But when the weather is nice, I really love taking a quiet walk in the park just to smell the green grass. It really helps me stay calm when our assignments start piling up.
Speaker 2 (Boy - Equipment): Ah, I’m completely the opposite! I need to keep running and use fitness equipment to burn off my stress. For me, it’s just so relaxing to exercise after lectures. It completely clears my head after sitting in a classroom all day.
Speaker 3 (Girl B - Passive): Wow, I’m definitely more passive. My favorite sports activity is literally just watching the Olympic matches on TV from my couch. Honestly, I'd rather just stay in the library and the cafe, and spend the whole afternoon reading books in a corner.
Speaker 1 (Girl A - Nature): Haha, reading is great, but I still try to enjoy the sunshine and do some stretch outside to get moving. I need to find much cheaper ways of keeping active.
Speaker 3 (Girl B - Passive): True, and honestly, the gym on campus gets more and more repetitive every time you go. Treadmills and weights get boring fast. Plus, our schoolwork is heavy this term, so I can't spend hours there. Just seeing green plants help relax my mind, or even cooking in the kitchen at home helps me unwind without any pressure.
Speaker 2 (Boy - Equipment): But wait, you don't need to spend a lot of money because the university has free facilities for us! There are plenty of low-cost options right on our doorstep. title: Free Online Courses 免费网课
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
Three academics are discussing free online courses and the reasons behind low enrollment numbers.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: Honestly, looking at the global data, it's amazing how many free online courses are available and really promising nowadays. They could be a total game-changer for higher education. But I honestly can hardly believe that so few people have enrolled this semester. The low participation and high drop rate across the board are just shocking to me.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: Well, I’m not entirely surprised. I think there's a major issue with initial trust here. When people see a platform offering a full syllabus for absolutely nothing, they immediately think it is too good to be true. They get deeply concerned about course quality, or worse, they suspect it is a scam or useless altogether.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: True, those doubts exist, but I think the bigger hurdle is practical rather than theoretical. It's not just about trust. Many students do not have time to commit to these programs because they are constantly juggling jobs and family obligations. They clearly have the desire to study, but the reality of a large amount of work in their daily lives stops them from finishing.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: That's a fair point, but don't get me wrong—online teaching requires a lot of design and deliver well. It requires a lot of effort from the faculty to set up. For individuals who cannot attend traditional school due to their difficult financial situation, these free platforms can be a lifeline! It’s such a very good idea, so it frustrates me that the completion rates are so abysmal.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: But that’s exactly the root of the problem. Because these modules are free, students face absolutely no financial punishment if they choose to quit halfway through. When a student pays thousands in tuition, they stay invested. Here, the only penalty is to yourself, which makes it way too easy to just walk away when things get busy. We really need to find other ways to build accountability in these virtual classrooms.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: Exactly, and we should also look at structural flexibility to accommodate their busy schedules. If universities could reschedule these courses to other times, like late evenings or weekends, we could easily attract more outsiders to join. Right now, a lack of promotion is also an issue; half the working professionals who need these skills don't even know these options exist.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: Mmm, I completely agree. Better scheduling and targeted marketing would definitely help pull in those outside demographics.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: Yeah! And we need to make sure the curriculum focuses on what they actually need. We want students to choose these modules because they are genuinely interested in it, and not because they are easy to pass. They need to see the real-world value, which is why we should design more practical over theoretical courses.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: Agreed. If we can fix the quality control, resolve the initial trust issues, and build a better framework for accountability, these free online courses might finally live up to their true potential.

title: Housing Plans 住宿计划 - 变体
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing their housing plans for the upcoming academic year.
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): Hey guys, I just got an alert from the accommodation office and it's making me completely stress out. I really need to weigh my options for next semester, but I'm kind of torn between my choices. I love the convenience of being close to classes, but I also really want more independence. Oh, by the way, Belle, can you remind me to pick up my laundry from the basement later? I keep forgetting.
Speaker 2 (On-Campus): Haha, yeah, I’ll text you later about the laundry. But about housing, I'm 100% coming back next year. In fact, I already put in my request for a single room on campus. I just think there’s a much better atmosphere for studying here. Plus, I absolutely hate commuting. The thought of waiting for the bus in the rain during a cold winter morning sounds completely miserable to me.
Speaker 3 (Off-Campus): Hmm, I see your point, but I'm strongly considering living outside the campus grounds this time. I definitely prefer a bit more independence than what the dorm rules allow. I actually found a pretty affordable place just a few blocks away, and it’s a great opportunity to experience more of the city rather than just staying inside the university bubble all day.
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): Ugh, you both make great points, which makes this even harder! I’m so nervous about submitting the response to the housing portal. They explicitly said room allocation is on a first-come basis, so I need to finalize my housing choice today if I want to beat the deadline.
Speaker 3 (Off-Campus): Well, why don't you sit down and make a list of pros and cons? That always helps me clear my head when I'm stuck. And hey, if you get completely desperate, you can always just flip a coin!
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): No way, I am not letting a coin decide where I live for a whole year!
Speaker 2 (On-Campus): Good call, don't do that. For me, looking at the stress of apartment hunting makes me even more set on staying in uni accommodation. Having 24/7 library access right down the hall is a lifesaver during exams. And honestly, not having to sign a lease or deal with standard landlords saves so much time. I can just focus on meeting up with my favorite study group.
Speaker 3 (Off-Campus): True, a legal contract is a big step. But my new place has a tiny kitchen, which I'm actually excited about. You guys should definitely come over for dinner once I get settled in. Right now, I'm figuring out how to cook tofu properly without it turning into a soggy mess. Hey, practice makes perfect, right?
Speaker 2 (On-Campus): Oh, count me in! I can bring some of my mom's homemade spice mix to help with that tofu experiment. Even though I love dorm life, going to your apartment will be a wonderful change of scenery for our weekend hangouts.
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): Wow, that spice mix sounds amazing. Okay, I think I'm starting to lean towards the dorms just to avoid the bus hassle, but man... that tiny kitchen dinner sounds great too. I'm going to run to the housing office right now before the clock runs out!

title: Student Exchange Program 交换生
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Two students and a student services officer are discussing applying for a student exchange programme at university.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): I’m really excited about applying for the student exchange programme next semester, guys, but oh my gosh... it looks like a huge amount of work. I logged onto the application website last night and the whole process just looks a bit overwhelming. I’m honestly terrified that I’m going to confuse the steps and miss some important deadlines.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Don't panic, Alice! It definitely seems like a lot to take in at first glance, but my job is to help you break it down into manageable steps. We provide clear checklists and info sessions throughout the month designed exactly to keep you on track so you don't miss a thing.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Phew, that makes me feel a bit better. I actually started poking around the portal last week, too. Right now, I'm just trying to pick a place, but I'm completely torn between three different countries. It's so hard to find a destination that offers a good academic fit for my major while also being somewhere I genuinely want to experience.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): To help narrow it down, Charlotte, your very first step should be looking into the credit transfer process. Our university has specific agreements with certain partner universities overseas. Because of this, you must work closely with academic advisor teams to ensure your course selections approved before you even book a flight.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Ah, right! That makes sense. I really want to go somewhere in Asia to get a completely different cultural experience, but I absolutely need to make sure those classes will count for my degree. I really can't afford to delay my graduation timeline.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Exactly. But besides the credits, my absolute biggest worry is the financial side of moving abroad. When you look at the overall cost of living in some of these host cities, plus the actual cost of flights and tuition, it starts to look completely out of reach for a student budget.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Oh, tell me about it! This isn’t just about saving up a small budget for a holiday; covering daily living expenses for a whole six months is a massive commitment. I’m already struggling financially with just my local expenses this semester, and I really don’t want to completely rely on my parents to bail me out.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Those are incredibly valid concerns, but that’s precisely why early financial planning is key. The university offers a variety of specialized scholarships and bursaries specifically to help offset travel costs for exchange students. There are even some external grants available if you look in the right places, but you need to apply early to secure them.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Wow, hearing that is seriously reassuring, Will. I had no idea the university offered that much support. I really want to do this programme for my own personal growth and independence, so knowing there are ways to manage the costs makes it feel worth the effort.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Me too! I'm much more motivated to tackle that overwhelming portal now.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Glad to hear it. Why don't you both come down to the global lounge for our official info session this Thursday? We can look at those checklists together and get your applications moving forward.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Perfect. I’ll definitely see you there.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Same here. Thanks a lot, Will!

title: Difficult Lecture 晦涩的讲座
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing what they feel about a course.
Speaker 1 (Confused): Ugh, gosh... that lecture was way too hard today. I mean, the professor was just jumping between different theories the whole time, and I could barely keep up with what he was saying. Look at my notebook—it’s just a complete jumble of scribbles. I was so lost that I think I even missed the part about next week's quiz.
Speaker 2 (Reader): Yeah, I saw you struggling. But honestly, it gets easier if you change your strategy. You really need to go through the reading list first, like, the night before class. Once you do that, the lecture makes a lot more sense because you already know the core vocabulary.
Speaker 3 (Librarian Helper): Exactly! And it's so easy to do now. Have you checked the new library website? Everything on the portal is perfectly organized by week, so you don't have to guess what's relevant. You can just search by title for any chapter you need.
Speaker 1 (Confused): I don't know, guys... the reading list is so long, it just stresses me out looking at it. I never know how to pick out the important parts. Yesterday, I gave up and spent an hour just scrolling through random websites trying to find shortcuts, but all those online summaries are too vague to actually help with our course.

title: Presentation Skills 演讲技巧（变型：Give Presentation）
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are chatting in the school library after class about how to improve presentation skills.
Speaker 1 (Anxious): Ugh, I'm already starting to feel overwhelmed about that upcoming assignment. We have a ten-minute presentation next week, and I just know I'm going to blank out in front of the whole class and completely embarrass myself. Every time I think about everyone staring at me, I completely freeze.
Speaker 2 (Practice/Mirror): Don't stress too much! Public speaking is super intimidating at first, but it all comes down to how you map things out. If you try to read from the script word by word, you'll inevitably sound like a robot, and the audience will feel bored within the first minute. For me, the whole point is to take notes instead of full paragraphs.
Speaker 3 (Eye Trick): Yeah, totally. I used to get so nervous that my voice would shake whenever I opened my mouth. A trick I learned is to completely avoid the audience's eyes if they throw you off. Instead, just look at their noses or foreheads. To the professors, it looks like you’re making perfect eye contact, but it takes away all the pressure!
Speaker 1 (Anxious): Wait, really? Just look at their foreheads? That sounds like an awesome life saver. My biggest fear is that if I don't have notes, I will completely freeze up, completely lose my train of thought, and just stand there and look like a fool. My natural instinct is always to try to memorize everything perfectly, but it's just exhausting.
Speaker 2 (Practice/Mirror): Trust me, memorization is a trap. If you drop one single sentence, it makes you panic, and it can make your speech too long if you ramble trying to find your spot. What you should do tonight is practice in front of a mirror. It really forces you to notice your body language. Developing these skills is so useful after graduation, especially when you're interviewing for an interview or pitching a project to a client.
Speaker 3 (Eye Trick): Exactly. And to keep your place without reading, you should place visual cues on your notes. I like to highlight the script using pens of different colors for different sections. A quick glance at a yellow or blue highlight tells you exactly where you are, which is amazing for building self-confidence on stage.
Speaker 1 (Anxious): Hmm... that color-coding method actually sounds manageable. So instead of a massive script, focusing on keywords and structure is the way to go? Just shifting my mindset to that makes me feel less anxious about the whole thing.
Speaker 2 (Practice/Mirror): Definitely! Tell you what, we can even record each other on our phones tomorrow afternoon to check our pacing. It’s a great intermediate step to help you slowly wean off notes until you just need small cue cards.
Speaker 3 (Eye Trick): That's a solid plan. Let's set up a small practice session in a study room tomorrow. To keep it something low-pressure, don't even worry about the class topic at first; just start by explaining a favorite book or a movie you love for a bit.
Speaker 1 (Anxious): Oh, I’d love that. I can easily prepare a short three-minute practice about a novel I just finished. If I can get comfortable doing that and practice using David's trick of looking at foreheads, I think I might actually come across as calm when the real day comes.
Speaker 2 (Practice/Mirror): You absolutely will. Let's lock in that study room for tomorrow, and we'll get this sorted out together!

title: Phone in Class 课上用手机
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three teachers are discussing whether students are allowed to use smartphones in class.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): I honestly think smartphones should be prohibited in our classrooms entirely. Every single day, my students are getting disturbed by texts vibrating on their desks, and this phenomenon really bothers me during lectures. It completely ruins the lesson flow. I want to stipulate that they must switch off their devices the moment they walk through the door.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): Oh, come on, a total ban is a bit extreme. We can actually teach them to use them for educational purposes. For instance, some of my foreign students check words on translation apps because they are not good at English yet. It actually helps them better understand what we teach, and it allows the class to be lively and interactive.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): True, but you have to admit it’s incredibly easy to get distracted by social media instead of studying. There are serious negative effects of constant multitasking on a student's brain. If we aren't careful, their concentration and grades will completely suffer.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): Exactly! It completely drives me crazy when they hide their screens under the desk and start chatting with others. As a teacher, you never know what they are doing down there! This screen addiction is everywhere now—just look at them playing on the phone during meals in the cafeteria. They don't know how to disconnect.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): Yeah, that’s a fair point. If we do allow them, it shouldn't turn into a free technology tutorial where we constantly waste lesson time trying to discourage them from scrolling. That's why consistency is key. If they can't use educational apps responsibly to do interactions, then devices should strictly be phones off and out of sight.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): But wait, we have to consider our own habits too. Sometimes teachers are glued to their own devices during break duties, and that hypocrisy sends a mixed message to the kids. Instead of fighting it, we should evolve with technology. If they need to look up information for a group project, let them use it, and then simply tell them to put it away after that.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): That sounds good in an ideal world, but it doesn't work in reality. We absolutely need a strict, school-wide policy so all students know they have to adhere to them across all subjects. I’m telling you, making them deposit their phones in a caddy at the entrance results in an immediate shift in focus and engagement. It forces everyone to realize we are part of the same learning community.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): Hmm... I wouldn't mind a designated phone storage area by the door if it’s handled flexibly. Why don't we pilot this in a few classes next term first? That way, we can see if students still get distracted without completely cutting off beneficial digital resources.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): Oh, I like that idea! If we pilot it, we can gather some research from our own trials to see if there's any improved student performance. It’s definitely not necessary to put a ban if we can find a middle ground. Let's present this proposal at the next staff meeting to get everyone on board.

title: Way to University 上学交通
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing the best ways to get to university.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Ugh, I absolutely hate taking the train now. Seriously, the train is always late, and the train company do nothing about it! It's driving me crazy. Honestly, I'm thinking about buying a car just so I can actually show up to morning classes on time.
Speaker 3 (Bike/Walk): Oh man, don't do it! Parking on campus is a nightmare though, and those gas costs add up fast. Trust me, a car is a massive money pit for a student.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Yeah, that's the problem. A car is way too expensive for me right now. Between trying to cover my tuition and rent, my budget is completely stretched. I’d probably need more part-time job shifts just to pay for petrol! But man, the train is even less reliable these days.
Speaker 2 (Bus Fan): Well, to be fair, I’ve never had that trouble with buses. I always take the first bus in the morning, and it’s honestly a great routine. It gives me plenty of time to prepare for my lectures and go over class materials before the campus gets chaotic.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Really? You can actually study on a bus?
Speaker 2 (Bus Fan): Yeah, totally! I usually just read academic articles or watch short study videos on my laptop. I really enjoy the quietness of the early morning commute. It’s a nice way to calm down before a busy day starts.
Speaker 3 (Bike/Walk): Wow, that sounds pretty peaceful, but I prefer being active. I actually run to school every day! It keeps me in shape and wakes me up instantly. Though, I am thinking about changing it up and wanting to try a bicycle soon, since cycling is great exercise too.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Huh, cycling? But what do you do when the weather turns awful? It must be so inconvenient on rainy days.
Speaker 3 (Bike/Walk): True, it can be a bit annoying. But I just wear a raincoat and always keep a foldable umbrella in my bag. If the downpour is completely crazy, I’ll just switch to the bus that day.
Speaker 2 (Bus Fan): That’s a sensible option. Just keep an eye on the clock though, because the road around campus is crowded during peak hours, and you can easily get stuck in the traffic if you leave too late.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Hmm... after hearing all this, I might actually be willing to try taking the bus next week. But what happens if the first bus is full?
Speaker 2 (Bus Fan): Oh, that does happen occasionally. If it’s packed, you just have to log into your phone and wait for the next one. That’s why having a backup plan is so crucial.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Right, makes sense. Maybe I should also look into buying a second-hand bicycle as my definitive backup plan, just in case the roads are completely blocked.
Speaker 3 (Bike/Walk): Hey, that’s a brilliant idea! There are some really good shops near campus that sell affordable used ones. I can show you where they are after class tomorrow if you like?
Speaker 2 (Bus Fan): Oh, nice! Let’s all do that. We can meet up early, grab a coffee before class, and then walk to the classroom together.
Speaker 1 (Train Hater): Haha, sounds like a solid plan. Thanks guys, anything is better than dealing with that train!

title: Field Trip 户外考察
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing whether they should take part in a field trip organized by the university.
Speaker 1 (Money Issue): I’m really torn about tomorrow's excursion, guys. My part-time shifts conflict with the field trip, and missing a full day of work is going to cost me a lot of money in lost wages. Since the trip is just an optional one, I think I’m just going to sit this one out and stick to my shift.
Speaker 2 (Organizer/Persuader): Oh, come on, don't say that! I took the bother to organize this group booking so we could all look in detail at the industries together. Plus, Business majors visit a hotel by sea to see how it is run, Geography students see beach cleanup, and since a History major visits history museum, it ties perfectly into my research on maritime trade. There is something for everyone!
Speaker 3 (Sports/Doubt): Honestly, I still see no point in going. Why should we visit a seashore hotel anyway? It just sounds like a glorified ad for the resort sponsor.
Speaker 1 (Money Issue): Exactly, that's what I was thinking.
Speaker 3 (Sports/Doubt): Plus, I have a really important football match tomorrow. I'm one of the team's starters, and my absence would drive the coach mad. I can’t just skip it.
Speaker 2 (Organizer/Persuader): But look at the academic benefits! It's a rare chance to learn a new style of hotel management that uses a completely different management than urban hotels, especially seeing how guests on the beach can raise many different requests. And Brian, wait—the history museum actually features a massive sports history section!
Speaker 3 (Sports/Doubt): Wait, really? A sports section?
Speaker 2 (Organizer/Persuader): Yes! They have archives on historical athlete nutrition trends. You could easily find relevant archives that might actually give your team an edge for the rest of the season.
Speaker 1 (Money Issue): You know, listening to all this makes me realize it's a great chance to socialize and meet more people outside my major. It would be a really nice change from my usual routine of just running between classes and work.
Speaker 3 (Sports/Doubt): That does sound a bit useful, actually. But don't get your hopes up just yet. I still have to double-check the timing with my team.
Speaker 1 (Money Issue): I think I’m going to try to swap my work shift after all. A coworker owes me a favor from last week, so I'll text her right now. Fingers crossed she says yes!
Speaker 2 (Organizer/Persuader): Brilliant! Let us know as soon as she replies.
Speaker 3 (Sports/Doubt): Alright, if you can swap your shift, Marcos, I'll go talk to the coach and see if I can manage both.

instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：

I think I’m definitely going to choose living in the dormitory next term. I’m actually quite excited to learn cooking, and I feel like the dorm is the perfect place to share food and make friends.
Speaker 2 (Uni Housing/Study): Same here! I’m staying in university housing too. Honestly, the convenience factor is unbeatable. title: Online Course 网课
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing the pros and cons of online classes.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): I was looking at our timetable options for next semester, and I seriously can't stand online classes anymore. During my last remote module, my Wi-Fi would also cut out constantly, and the presentation slides freeze all the time. On top of that, I kept getting distracted by my phone, so I ended up missing half the content because I couldn't focus on the screen.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): That's a shame, but I actually prefer online learning over sitting in a crowded lecture theatre. For one thing, there's no more rushing out the door just to catch the 8am bus. I don't have to waste time commuting, and there is no spending money on cafeteria food either. I can just attend class in my pajamas and focus on taking notes in my comfortable room.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): I get the convenience, but I chose this university for the campus experience, not to stare at little boxes on a screen all day. When everything is remote, it feels like we are all just lost in the digital void. I definitely learn better through face-to-face interactions because you can actually read body language and feed off the dynamic classroom energy.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): You have to consider the flexibility it offers, though. If you don't grasp a concept immediately, you can easily review lecture recordings later, even while eating dinner. It saves me nearly two hours every day on travel alone. Because of that comfort, I actually feel less intimidated and participate more online than I ever would in person.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): That might work for some, but I really value engaging in person. In a real classroom, if I have a question, I can just raise my hand and get immediate answers, whereas last week I typed a query in the chat and the professor didn't see it at all. Plus, real group discussions are so much better. Online breakout rooms are just awkward and unproductive, usually filled with dead silence and blank screens.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): Exactly, those blank screens make it impossible to make friends or network properly. I actually failed a course last year when it was fully remote because I couldn't stay motivated alone. That’s why I strongly favor a hybrid over fully online approach. Having a schedule that is primarily in-person ensures we still get some campus experience while keeping things organized.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): A hybrid model could be a fair compromise, I suppose. It still allows those who live far away to study in their comfortable room for part of the week while avoiding the daily mad rush. As long as we can still access the recorded material to rewatch difficult parts, I think it balances the saving of time and money quite well.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): I could live with a hybrid system as long as the core seminars are face-to-face. I just need that external environment to keep me away from being distracted by my phone. Having real, spontaneous group discussions without technical glitches like frozen slides making us miss half the content is crucial for my learning.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): Definitely. A hybrid model with a primarily in-person focus seems like the best path forward. It keeps us from getting lost in the digital void, lets us absorb that dynamic classroom energy, and ensures we don't miss out on the genuine university life we all signed up for. Let's make sure we select the blended streams when enrollment opens.

title: The Final Exam 期末考试
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are debating the value of final exams versus continuous assessment.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): I was just looking over our syllabus for next term, and it really got me thinking—final exams feel so outdated these days. Last semester was an absolute nightmare for me because I had three finals on the same day. I felt completely overwhelmed with memorizing facts, formulas, and dates just to pass. It felt more like a memory test than actual education.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): You're so right, and those traditional exams just encourage cramming the night before, which doesn't help us retain knowledge long-term. Instead of written tests, we should be assigned projects or research papers. Working on real-world projects forces us to think critically about the subject matter rather than just skimming through textbook chapters for a grade.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): I see your points, but look at it this way—finals definitely serve a purpose in our academic development. Preparing for a massive exam forces us to review the entire semester's content from start to finish. It’s a highly valuable opportunity to consolidate everything we’ve learned into a big, cohesive picture before moving on to the next year.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): That sounds good in theory, but the extreme pressure actually causes many students to forget everything a week after the test is over. So many of my classmates suffer from severe anxiety because of this. Plus, traditional exams feel isolating and artificial, unlike real-world projects that allow for creativity and collaboration.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): Exactly! Building on your point about isolation, the stress is often so intense that you can just panic and completely blank during the exam itself. I realized afterwards that I didn't truly understand most of what I wrote down. Judging a student's entire semester based solely on their performance under pressure like that is simply not real learning.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): That might happen to some, but completing a major final exam also gives you a fantastic sense of closure at the end of the term. Walking out of that exam hall brings a massive sense of accomplishment. Furthermore, studying for them helps teach discipline and crucial time management skills that we'll always need in our careers.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): Well, I still believe that utilizing diverse evaluation methods would create a more equitable system for everyone, especially those who excel practically. After all, when we finally step into the real world, our employers will ask us to deliver successful projects, not sit quietly for standardized tests.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): Absolutely, which is why a continuous assessment model would be much better because we could absorb material gradually week by week. Exams turn our education into a high-stakes game where one bad day completely ruins your GPA. We should focus on achieving a deep understanding of concepts instead of just regurgitating information on a test sheet.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): To be fair, from an institutional view, exams are necessary because they are efficient for grading fairly. A standardized exam is an objective way to review the full scope of a student's knowledge while maintaining academic standards. However, I do agree that a mix of both methods would probably work best for a balanced curriculum.

title: Management of Assignment 作业规划
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：

 Three students are discussing strategies for managing their written assignments.



Speaker 1: Honestly guys, I’ve been feeling a lot of pressure lately because I find it hard to organize everything for our upcoming courses. Every single time I write a goal down, I just cannot stick to it for long. I never do it consistently, and I always end up losing momentum halfway through, which completely stalls my progress.

Speaker 2: I used to have that exact problem until I started using a breakdown method. Now, whenever we get lengthy assignments, I immediately break them into smaller ones. I make a plan, create an outline, and schedule everything step by step. Dealing with bite-sized tasks makes the workload feel much less intimidating.

Speaker 3: That's a solid strategy. For me, I prefer a routine-based method where I allocate different amounts of time depending on whether a task is urgent or difficult. I also try to work when I feel the most productive. Personally, I work best at night, especially in the evening after dinner when things quiet down.

Speaker 1: I wish I could do that, but I keep getting sidetracked by the smallest things, and then my whole plan falls apart. I think I'm really missing an external structure in my life. Without someone checking in on me, I just don't have that immediate accountability to keep my head down and focus.

Speaker 2: Distractions are definitely the enemy. If you get distracted, it will take longer to finish anything. That's why when I follow my schedule, I actively avoid mobile phones, TV, and checking emails. It requires a structured yet flexible approach, but making a conscious effort to try to focus without technology nearby helps immensely.

Speaker 3: Absolutely, and sticking to that routine is what helps you stay consistent and avoid last-minute stress. By setting mini-deadlines for each part of the work, you aren't rushing at the end. I’ve noticed that when I don't leave things to the final hour, it significantly improves the overall quality of my work.

Speaker 1: You both make excellent points. This is exactly why I think I need to have a work buddy. Having someone working right next to me would give me that vital sense of responsibility. If we push each other, I won't get sidetracked as easily, and it will force me to build better habits.

Speaker 2: That is a fantastic idea! Why don't we do the next assignment together? We can plan together and get motivated, and we can even practice as a group. Combining my step-by-step strategy with your need for a study partner sounds like a perfect win-win situation to keep us all on track.

Speaker 3: I’m completely on board with that. Having a study group is perfect because it keeps us accountable to one another. Plus, we can share ideas and feedback on each other's work before submitting it. It gives Speaker 1 the external structure they need while helping all of us maintain consistency. Let's do it!

title: Extension for Work 申请延期
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing whether they will ask their professor for more time to do an essay.
Speaker 1: Hey guys, I am absolutely scrambling to finish my philosophy essay right now. The deadline approaches in just a few hours, and the timing is going to be really tight. It’s a total mad rush, last minute as per usual for me. I honestly don't know why I never seemed to plan ahead properly, but now I'm stuck dealing with the panic.
Speaker 2: Don't worry, you're not alone—I am completely in the same boat. I have a literal mountain of work to do because I have multiple essays due tomorrow! I totally messed up the dates and accidentally wrote next Monday in my diary. Now it's too late to ask for help, and I’m facing extremely limited time to get all this research done.
Speaker 3: Oh wow, that sounds incredibly stressful for both of you. I was facing a similar nightmare because I have a huge load of assignments due all at once this week, and to make things worse, I’m currently packing to move house. It’s been such a difficult juggle, but luckily, I asked for an extension and got an extra couple of days.
Speaker 1: You're so lucky to get that extra time. For me, it's way too late to ask my professor now, so I’ve just got to push through the night and finish it. The biggest bummer is that I won't be able to watch the football match tonight. I seriously need to learn my lesson about procrastination after this.
Speaker 2: Yeah, it’s definitely too late for me to ask too. But honestly, even if I could, I sometimes feel like an extension just prolongs the pain. It just drags it out over the whole weekend when you could be relaxing. Since my time is limited anyway, I’d rather just lock myself in the library tonight, focus, and make it happen.
Speaker 3: I see your point about not wanting to drag it out, but with my house move, I really needed the break. I don't want to sound ungrateful, but I actually would have liked a longer extension. However, my professor leaves for her sabbatical next week, so she couldn't give me more time. Still, it's better than nothing.
Speaker 1: That’s fair enough, at least you got some relief. Our professors are usually more understanding if you have a genuine excuse like moving. As for me, I have to accept my fate. Missing the football game sucks, but I just need to break this habit of working at the last minute and get this philosophy paper done.
Speaker 2: Exactly, no more distractions for us. Since my essays are due tomorrow morning, there's no point crying over messing up the dates in my diary. I just need to tackle this mountain of work head-on tonight and make it happen. Once it's submitted, the stress will finally be over.
Speaker 3: That's the spirit! I’m going to go put my head down now and start writing as well. Even with the extra couple of days, I can't afford to waste time with all my packing. We've got this, and remember, handing in a rushed paper is still a hundred times better than not handing anything in at all.

title: Online Lectures 上网课的感受
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the pros and cons of online classes.

"I really can't stand online classes. Last week during my economics lecture, I kept getting distracted by my phone and ended up missing half the content. And when I tried to ask a question in the chat, the professor didn't see it until the next day!"

"Actually, I prefer online learning. Think about it - no more rushing to catch the 8am bus, no spending money on cafeteria food, and I can attend class in my pajamas. I just open my notebook and focus on taking notes. The recorded lectures are great too - I can rewatch difficult parts anytime."

"But that's exactly the problem! I chose this university for the campus experience. How am I supposed to make friends or network if we're all just little boxes on a screen? And when I type a question, by the time the professor responds, we've already moved on to another topic."

"Exactly! In physical classes, I can just raise my hand and get immediate answers. Plus, group discussions are so much more engaging in person. Online breakout rooms always feel awkward and unproductive."

"I get your point about socializing, but consider the flexibility. I can review lecture recordings while eating dinner, or study in my comfortable room instead of those hard library chairs. And honestly, I find I actually participate more online - I'm too shy to speak up in big lecture halls."

"That might work for you, but I learn better through face-to-face interactions. Body language and classroom energy help me understand the material. Last semester I failed a course because the online format just didn't work for my learning style."

"Same here! At least in physical classes, the professor can see when students look confused. Online, they just keep lecturing to blank screens. Maybe a hybrid system would be better - some online, some in-person classes?"

"That could be a good compromise. We'd get the benefits of both formats. Though I'd still prefer fully online - it saves me nearly two hours of commuting every day."

"Well, I'd take hybrid over fully online any day. At least that way I could still get some of the campus experience. But honestly, I think education should be primarily in-person - that's what university is all about, right?"

"Agreed. Maybe the solution is offering both options and letting students choose what works best for them."

title: How to Write An Essay 如何写好论文
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the difficulties they are having with writing an essay.

You're welcome! Just remember to take it one step at a time. Writing an essay doesn't have to be a huge, insurmountable task. You're capable of breaking it down and conquering it, piece by piece.

title: Attending an Evening Event 是否参加晚间活动
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing whether to attend an evening event.

Have you two heard about the evening event this Friday? I really think we should go. Everyone seems to be talking about it, and I've heard so many good things already. There will be a DJ show, dance performances, live music, and all kinds of activities. It sounds like one of the biggest events of the semester, and I don't want to miss it.

To be honest, I wasn't planning to go. I don't usually attend live events like that. Most of the time, I'd rather stay at home and watch television. It feels more relaxing to me. And I don't really enjoy large crowds.

Actually, I'd really like to go. The event sounds fun. And I haven't been to anything like this for a while. The problem is that I have a design course project to finish. I've been working on it all week. And there's still a lot left to do.

Come on, I think you're both overthinking it. Events like this don't happen very often. It's a great chance to relax, meet people, and enjoy something different from our usual routine. Even if you only stay for a couple of hours, it'll be worth it.

You know what? You've actually convinced me. The DJ show and performances do sound interesting. And maybe it would be nice to do something different for a change. Alright, I'll come with you.

I wish I could join you. But I really need to focus on my design course. I don't think I'll have enough time before the deadline. It's a shame because I was looking forward to the event. Anyway, if you do go, make sure you take lots of photos. And tell me all about it afterwards.

Deal. We'll take plenty of photos and videos for you. Hopefully next time you'll be free to come along with us.

title: Sociology Conference 社会学会议
discussion_text:
Two students and a tutor are discussing their presentation at a sociology conference.

Hey, I was just thinking about you two attending the sociology conference next week—I’m really excited for you! So, how’s your preparation going? 

Actually, we were thinking of doing a joint presentation at the conference. We feel our topics overlap quite a bit, and presenting together might make for a stronger session.

Yeah, even though our topics are a bit different, there are actually quite a lot of common points in our study, so we thought it would be great to share ideas and build on each other’s work.

Well, to be honest, I have a few reservations because neither of you has the experience—it can be quite challenging. But since you're set on doing a joint presentation, here’s what I suggest: let’s organize a practice presentation. I’ll sit in as an observer, and we can invite a few other students to join the audience. That way, you’ll get the constructive feedback you need before the real conference.

That sounds like a great plan! We’re definitely going to prep a practice presentation. We’re really eager to get your feedback, because we know it’ll help us deliver a much stronger presentation at the actual conference.

Yeah, a practice presentation is definitely a great idea. Actually, I was planning to get your approval before making the final decision to attend the conference anyway. So, this session aligns perfectly with my original plan. Plus, since our research is still in the early stages, getting that feedback now would be really valuable for us.

title: Compulsory Summer Classes 强制暑期课程
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the university’s new academic calendar policy. The academic calendar has been changed, and summer is now being used for compulsory classes.

Have you heard? The school might introduce a new academic calendar. Apparently, summer could be used for compulsory classes in the future. I was really surprised when I saw the announcement this morning.

Yeah, I heard about it too. Honestly, I’m a bit worried because I already arranged an internship for the summer, and other people have probably made plans as well. A lot of students rely on the summer break to gain work experience.

Exactly. Many internships can only be arranged during the summer, so this policy could make us miss out on valuable internship opportunities. Employers usually expect students to be available during that period.

I understand your point. I haven’t planned anything myself yet, but I was hoping for a more flexible summer—like being able to travel, relax a little, or spend time with family before the next semester starts.

From what I know, the school is only asking for feedback at the moment. The policy probably won’t be implemented until a few years later. If it really happens, though, we’d probably end up having nine breaks throughout the year instead of one long summer vacation. Also, I can also understand the school’s perspective. If summer classes are not compulsory, some students may lack self-discipline at home and end up wasting time instead of studying productively.

discussion_text:
Three speakers are discussing the new experience at university. 

Hey everyone! Can’t believe we’ve been at university for a month already. How’s everyone feeling about it? I come from a small town where there wasn’t much to do—mostly just watching movies or playing football with friends. But now that I’m here in the big city, everything feels so fresh and exciting.

For me, university life hasn’t brought any huge changes compared with my past life. I’m actually from a big city, so when I was in high school, my friends often organized all kinds of activities and gatherings. But I wasn’t really the outgoing type. I seldom went out and didn’t enjoy taking part in those social or entertainment activities very much.

I totally get you. There are just so many activities going on, both on and off campus. After joining them, I often feel really worn out and don’t have the energy to review my lessons, let alone finish my homework. I can only get a proper rest on weekends or during holidays.

Well, I think the most important thing is to find a balance between university activities and study. I usually finish my urgent study tasks right after class before going out to have fun. That way, I never let my important work get delayed.

Mine’s a bit different! I usually hang out on weekdays and save homework, laundry and house chores for the weekends. Sometimes I’ll go to my friends’ parties on Saturday nights if there’s one on, it’s a nice little break!

title: Social Media 社交媒体
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing whether social media does more harm than good to university students.

Have you noticed how much time we all spend on social media every day? I think it's become a real problem-it's distracting, affects mental health, and keeps people from having real conversations. I've seen people cancel plans just to stay home and scroll through feeds, which really worries me.

I totally agree. A lot of students end up comparing themselves to others online, which just makes them anxious or unhappy. Not to mention how easy it is to waste hours scrolling instead of studying or actually hanging out with friends. Just last week, I lost three hours watching random videos when I should have been finishing an essay.

Actually, I don't see it that way. Social media helps me stay connected with friends from home, join student groups, and even find academic opportunities. It's all about how you use it--it can be a tool, not just a distraction. For example, I stick to just one platform and only turn on notifications for an hour daily to avoid constant distractions.

Well, I don’t agree with this idea, as it could make you miss crucial information. Besides, even if you try every possible way not to be disturbed, the algorithms are designed to keep you hooked. Even if you start with good intentions, it's easy to fall into endless scrolling. And don't forget about privacy issues or misinformation. Once you click on one controversial topic, your feed gets flooded with similar content-it's hard to escape.

Yeah, and it often replaces face-to-face interaction. I've seen people sitting together in the cafe, everyone on their phone instead of talking. It kinda defeats the purpose of being on campus, doesn't it? We're losing the ability to read body language and have deep, spontaneous conversations.

I understand the concerns, but banning or overly criticizing social media isn't the answer. We should focus on digital literacy teaching people how to use these platforms responsibly. It's part of modern life, and we need to learn to navigate it. We could host student-led workshops on setting boundaries and curating a positive online experience.

That's a fair point. Maybe the issue isn't social media itself, but how we use it. If used intentionally, it doesn't have to be negative. But without proper education, most people won't use it intentionally- they will just consume.

True. Balance and self-control are key. Maybe the university could offer workshops on healthy digital habits instead of just telling us to log off. Learning to use tech mindfully is a skill, just like time management or critical thinking.

Now that's something I could support. Guidance is better than restriction. Let's make technology work for us, not against us. Maybe we can propose a "Digital Wellness Week" through the student union to raise awareness.

title: Commuting to the University 上学的交通方式
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the best way to commute to the university.

Good morning! It seems you are late today. I suggest that you try to leave earlier next time.

Yeah, I know. I have been late three times. I hate taking the train to university. It’s always late! This train is the first train each morning, and it only comes once a day. Plus, I live a little far away from our campus, so I really have no other choice. I always get up early in order to catch it, but because the train company does nothing to improve the service to ensure the train arrives on time, I’m still late for class.

I understand your frustration. Have you ever thought about buying a car? That will make your commuting more flexible.

Yes, I have. I'm considering buying a car, but it’s just too expensive. So, I have to save money for it. I need to take on more part-time work to cover the cost. But for now, maybe I should look into carpooling or even rent a car first instead of buying my own car. It’s more affordable for me right now.

Well, I don’t think driving a car to school is a good choice. I often see traffic jams, and those cars are waiting at long traffic lines on the road. How do you usually go to school?

I take the bus to campus, which I don’t think is a wise choice either. Like, a bus may be stuck in traffic sometimes and the buses are always crowded and busy. But the good thing about public transport is that I can use the time productively - I often read articles and go over class materials on my way to school. It helps me prepare for classes or just catch up on reading.

You are right about buses getting stuck in traffic. That's why I prefer riding my bike to school. It's a great exercise, and I don't have to worry about train delays or traffic jams. I can always predict exactly how long my commute will take, and I arrive feeling energized from the ride. Plus, it's much cheaper than any other option.

That does sound convenient, but I live too far away to bike. I guess each commuting option has its advantages and disadvantages. For example, what would you do when it’s rainy?

Easy! Just put on a jacket or switch to the bus that day! Oh, that reminds me! Maybe you could combine biking with public transport? Many buses have bike racks these days. And if the bus doesn’t work out, like if the first bus is full, the bicycle is still a backup. I used to cycle to school when I lived a little farther away, and the distance didn’t bother me at all. And if you need help picking out a bicycle, just tell me _ I know a few good shops near campus that sell affordable used ones!

Yay, that’s a good call! I think I’ll start with the first bus next week, and if it doesn’t work, I’ll look into buying a second-hand bicycle. It’s way cheaper than buying a car, and I could take it as extra exercise, too. More importantly, no more being late!

title: Environmentally Friendly University 环境友好型大学
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing what the university can do to reduce its environmental impacts.

Have you noticed the new recycling bins around campus? I think they’re a good idea because they should help reduce the amount of waste going to landfill. If recycling bins are available in more places, it will also be easier for students to recycle their waste properly.

That’s true, but I think we should reduce waste from the source. Instead of simply having more recycling bins, we should try to reduce the amount of waste produced in the first place. That would probably have a greater environmental impact in the long term.

I agree, especially when you look at the waste from the cafeteria. The cafeteria uses recycled paper, which is good, but sometimes they give out too many pieces at one time. There’s also far too much packaging on some of the food. I remember seeing an apple with several layers of packaging around it, which seemed completely unnecessary.

Coffee cups are another problem. People should use fewer single-use coffee cups in the café. Students could bring their own reusable cups instead. The university could also encourage more people to do that.

We should also think about more sustainable transportation. For example, the university could build better bike paths so that more students feel comfortable cycling to campus. It should also provide more bike parking around the university. That would make cycling much more convenient for students.

Another option is to encourage carpooling. A lot of students drive to university by themselves, so sharing a car could reduce the number of cars coming onto campus. The university could offer cheaper parking to students who carpool, or maybe even give them free parking. That would be a good way to reward students for making a more environmentally friendly choice.

I like the idea of carpooling. It doesn’t just reduce the environmental impact. Carpooling also allows students to get together and travel to university with other people. So there’s a social benefit as well.

Public transport could be improved as well. If there were better buses or trains to the university, fewer students might need to drive. That would give students another sustainable way to travel to campus.

So there are actually a lot of things the university can do to reduce its environmental impact. But I think we should also start with small things ourselves. We can bring our own cups to the cafeteria, recycle properly, or carpool with other students. If everyone makes a few small changes, together they could make a big difference.

title: Draft Assignment 作业草稿
discussion_text:
Two students and a tutor are discussing their draft assignments.

Hi tutor, I’ve run into a really tricky problem while working on my essay. I always end up spending hours and writing way too much. But when I go back to check it, I still feel like it’s not enough—many key points aren’t covered, and my ideas aren’t clearly expressed.

Oh, I totally agree with you! I always try to include every single detail of my ideas, and I end up almost exceeding the word limit.

Well, I totally understand your frustration. Maybe you just need to focus more on the context of the question. Trying to put every single detail in doesn’t ensure a high score. It’ll be all right as long as your ideas are well-organized and directly answer the question.

Well, the problem is mainly with your structure—keeping repeating the same points throughout your writing is a typical sign of an unclear structure. I suggest you start the assignment by making a clear draft before you write. Don’t worry too much when doing the outline, though; this is only your first draft. You can revise it and reorganize your ideas, and then submit it once you’ve made those changes.

Oh, I finally understand what you mean, tutor. I will plan my essay structure before I start writing. I will focus on the key points and use a clear, direct way to explain why they are important. In this way, I think I can successfully reduce repeated points that I was just explaining in different ways.

Yeah, thank you so much for your advice, tutor. I really appreciate you listening to us patiently and giving us such clear and useful feedback.

title: Seaside Field Trip 海边户外教学
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing a field trip at university.

Hey guys, I just heard that the school is organizing a field trip next month, but the thing is, I’m not even sure where exactly we’re going. And honestly, I’ve got a part-time job on weekends, and I really need money from this job, so I’m wondering—do you know if this field trip is optional?

Yeah, actually, this field trip is optional. But you know, I really feel we could learn a lot from it, otherwise why would the school bother to organize it, right? Like, business and tourism students will go visit seaside hotels, geology and geography students will observe shells and rocks, and the history students will tour the maritime museum.

Hmm, well, I’m really not interested in seaside hotels. I mean, there are already a lot of hotels in the city, and to me they all seem pretty much the same. I don’t see what’s so exciting about them.

I don’t think so. They’re actually different in many ways—for example, seaside hotels have a totally different customer base, facilities, and even design compared to city hotels. I think you could really learn a lot if you look closely. Don’t you want to look in detail?

Alright, fair enough. But personally, I’m really interested in the maritime museum. It sounds fascinating. And besides, I think it would be a great chance to meet new people. Right now, you are the only people I know in the business class, so this feels like a good opportunity to go together.

Oh, you’re right—I hadn’t thought about the chance to meet new people. That’s actually a good point. And now that I think of it, I’m also quite interested in the maritime museum. I’d really like to see it. Maybe I could try to change shifts, like switch some work to weekdays. That way I could still join. Honestly, I think this would be a good idea to go on a field trip outside the campus.

title: The Development of AI AI的发展
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the development of AI.

Hey, have you guys been following all the buzz around AI lately? I'm honestly feeling pretty excited about it—especially with things like generative AI and how it's changing creative work. I've been experimenting with some tools, and it's amazing what you can create now. Last week, I even used AI to write code and design posters! 

I mean, sure, AI's great for getting certain things done—especially the simple, repetitive stuff. But when it comes to complex tasks that need real judgment or creativity? That's still on us. Humans bring understanding and context that AI just can't replicate. 

Honestly, I'm kind of worried. What if AI keeps taking over and there are fewer jobs out there? I mean, entry-level positions are already disappearing. I'm scared that by the time I graduate, there won't be much left for new grads like us.

I wouldn't worry too much if I were you. Yeah, some jobs might disappear, but new ones always pop up—probably ones we can't even imagine yet. Think about it: a decade ago, who'd heard of AI prompt engineers or social media managers? There'll be tons of new roles created. We just have to stay adaptable and keep learning.

Yeah, AI's definitely going to bring a lot of convenience. Imagine not having to deal with all those boring, repetitive tasks—it could handle the grunt work so we can focus on what actually matters. Honestly, I think it'll make life easier in ways we're just starting to see.

Yeah, I totally agree there are benefits—like how AI saves so much time on repetitive tasks. For example, in healthcare, AI is helping doctors diagnose faster and more accurately. It's already making a real difference in ways we couldn't have imagined a few years ago.

title: Keeping Active at University 在学校里保持锻炼
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing how to keep active at university.

Hi everyone, I was thinking we should have a discussion about university activities. I've been considering getting more involved on campus, but I find that joining clubs is too expensive. The membership fees are really high, and when you add up all the costs throughout the semester, it becomes a significant amount. And that's not all - parking is expensive too, especially if you need to drive to campus regularly for activities. So I'm trying to figure out how to be active and social without spending too much money. I'd really like to hear your ideas to save money while still enjoying university life. What do you both think about this situation?

That's a really good topic to discuss. From my perspective, I believe the university has many free facilities that students sometimes overlook. When I'm looking for activities, I prefer low-cost options that don't require much spending. A great option is swimming - the campus pool is accessible with our student ID. And sometimes, the simplest choice is just going for a walk around campus. I think these activities are relaxing and budget-friendly choices that don't put pressure on your finances. You can enjoy yourself without worrying about the cost.

I completely understand where you're coming from. Personally, I feel my schoolwork is heavy with lots of assignments and classes this semester, so I need affordable ways to unwind. What works well for me is walking around campus, especially in the green areas. I find that walking and seeing green plants helps me relax and clear my mind after long study sessions. It's a simple pleasure that doesn't cost anything. Additionally, I also enjoy cooking in the kitchen - preparing simple meals helps me take a break from academic work and restore energy for the next day's study. These activities help me manage the workload without adding financial stress.

Thank you both for sharing those suggestions. After hearing others' suggestions, I'm starting to see some good alternatives. Actually, I think I've decided to go to the university swimming pool as my main activity. It sounds like a healthy option that fits within my budget. Plus, I remember someone mentioning that the pool is Olympic-standard and professional, which makes it even more appealing. It's impressive that we have access to such a high-quality facility without extra cost.

That sounds like an excellent decision. And since we're talking about making the most of this activity, I'd like to add one more suggestion: you could bring some snacks with you or drink a cup of coffee after swimming. This can make the experience more enjoyable and help you relax even further. It's still a budget-friendly approach, especially if you bring your own snacks from home or use your student discount at the campus café.

title: Accommodation Next Year 明年住宿问题
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the accommodation options next academic year.

Hey guys, I was wondering if you've made any decisions about where you're planning to live next academic year? I know the housing application deadlines are coming up soon, and I'm still trying to weigh my options between staying in university accommodation or finding a private flat.

Actually, I just signed a contract yesterday for a studio apartment in the city center, and I couldn't be more relieved! After a full year in the noisy dormitory, I'm really looking forward to having my own quiet space. What I hated most about dorm life was the constant disturbance - people coming and going at all hours, loud music in the evenings, and the worst part was definitely sharing kitchen facilities. I'm quite particular about my food, and it drove me crazy when people would help themselves to things from my shelf in the fridge. This new place is slightly more expensive, but for me, having that privacy and peace is absolutely worth the extra cost.

That's interesting because my experience has been completely the opposite! I've actually grown to love dormitory living, especially because of the shared kitchen. Cooking has always been my passion, and I've found it's such a wonderful way to connect with people from different cultures. Just last week, my French roommate taught me how to make authentic crêpes, and in return I showed her some traditional dishes from my country. Those spontaneous cooking sessions often turn into great conversations where we learn so much about each other's backgrounds. For me, that cultural exchange is one of the most valuable parts of university life that I'd miss in private accommodation.

I have to agree with staying in university housing, though for slightly different reasons. The convenience factor is unbeatable - my dorm is literally a three-minute walk from all my lecture halls. When I have 9am classes, I can wake up at 8:45 and still make it on time! But more importantly, I've found the academic support system invaluable. During exam periods last semester, we organized nightly study groups in the common room where we could quiz each other and explain difficult concepts. That collaborative environment really helped boost my grades in ways I don't think would have happened if I was living alone off-campus.

title: Reading Before Class 课前阅读
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing how to finish reading before class.

Ugh, I don't know about you guys, but I think today's lecture was way too hard and I could barely keep up with what the professor was saying.

Yeah, I get what you mean. But honestly, I think it gets easier if you go through the reading list first. The professor mentioned those books for a reason. If you read them before class, the lecture will be much easier to follow.

Hmm, maybe. But the reading list is so long! I don't even know where to find all these books and articles!

Well, actually, it's pretty easy to find those books on the library website. They usually have all the course readings listed there, organized by week, and you can just search by title. Oh, and most of them have PDF previews, so you can flip through the contents to see which chapters the professor highlighted.

Oh, really? I didn't know that. I’ve been wasting time scrolling through random website pages. Most of them don't match what the professor talked about. I should have checked the library first instead of struggling with those.

It’s totally fine—half the class didn’t realize the library had all this stuff at first. And most importantly, if you get stuck, the librarian is super helpful. Last week, I couldn't find one of the recommended articles, and she showed me exactly how to access it online, using the library‘s archive database.

Oh that's useful! Thanks for sharing. And with all the reading materials available now, I'm more convinced that reading before class is important. If you read ahead, you're not going to fall behind during the lecture. And trust me, once you've read them, the lecture won't feel half as hard.

Yes, now that I know the library’s that easy to use and the reading list actually lines up with the lectures. I'll go to check the library website tomorrow, and maybe talk to the librarian if I get lost.

Good plan. Once you get used to it, finding the readings is pretty quick. I used to spend hours stressing over it, but now I can pull up what I need in 10 minutes. Also you can bookmark the course page so you don‘t have to hunt for it every time.

title: Different Types of Classes不同类型的课堂
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing different types of classes at university.

There are no lectures in high school, so coming to university was quite a big change for me. Most of the classes at university are lectures, and sometimes I find them difficult to follow. Some teachers speak very fast, and a few of them have strong accents, which makes it even harder to understand everything they say.

Personally, I like lectures. One advantage is that teachers usually upload their PowerPoint slides online, so if you miss a lecture or don't catch everything during class, you can always check the slides later. However, I think tutorials have their own advantages as well. The best thing about tutorials is that you can ask questions and have discussions, whereas in a large lecture it is often difficult to ask questions during the class.

I don't really like lectures either. They are simply too long. Sometimes a lecture lasts for an hour, and sometimes even ninety minutes. It can be very difficult to stay focused on one person speaking for such a long period of time. That's why I prefer tutorials. Most of the tutors I've met are very patient, and I've had really positive experiences in those classes.

I agree with that. Tutorials are usually more interactive, and it's much easier to get help when you need it. Even if you don't want to ask questions during the class, you can always stay behind and ask the tutor afterwards. They are usually happy to explain things again or give extra guidance.

title: Large Group Lectures 大班课
discussion_text:
Three students are having a group discussion about large group lectures.

Lily, you didn’t attend the large group lecture this morning, right? The professor was really unhappy about that. You were supposed to sign the attendance sheet—it’s an important part of our course assessment. Later, the teacher will email you and ask you to clarify this matter.

Oh, I know. But honestly, I just can’t stand those large group lectures. They are so boring! The professor just reads notes the whole time, and I can do that at home by myself. I can read the course notes, watch the recorded video of the lecture, and even review the key points more efficiently without sitting in the crowded classroom. To be honest, I prefer group discussions and seminars much more. They are way more interesting and interactive. We can share our ideas, ask questions, and learn from each other, which is much more helpful than just listening to someone read notes.

I get what you mean—large lectures can be tedious sometimes. But even so, you still need to attend them. When we all go to the lecture, we learn the same content at the same time. After that, we can discuss the same questions with our course mates, clarify our doubts together, and make sure we all understand the key knowledge points correctly. It’s hard to do that if we all study separately at home.

Exactly! Besides, in this digital age, we already have very little face-to-face interaction with people. Most of our communication is online—chatting through messages or having online meetings. The large group lecture is a good chance for us to meet our course mates and professor face to face, which helps us build better relationships with them.

Hmm, I never thought about the physical reaction part before. But I still think the lectures could be more engaging. Maybe if the professor added more discussions instead of just reading notes, more students would be willing to attend.

I totally get you. I prefer seminars to lectures as well. But from the school’s perspective, it’s much cheaper to have one professor teach 100 students in a large group lecture than to have the same professor teach only 10 students in a small class. That’s probably why the school arranges so many large group lectures—it’s a cost-effective way to deliver the course content to all students.
