title: Prepare for Final Exams 准备期末考试
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing preparing for final exams at university.

Oh man, I'm already feeling the pressure for finals. It feels like there's just so much to cover and, like, so little time. I'm trying to figure out the best way to deal with everything, especially for that quantitative methods exam. I really need to ace that one.

I know exactly what you mean, Will. I've started making detailed study schedules, blocking out specific times for each subject. For quantitative methods, I've found that doing past papers with a timer on really helps make the concepts stick. It's tough, but it helps you see your weak spots quickly.

That's a good strategy, Lily, but sometimes I find past papers just stress me out more if I'm not confident with the material first. I've been focusing more on active recall and spaced repetition, especially for my history courses. It's basically like quizzing yourself all the time, and then going back to topics after longer and longer periods. It feels like it helps more with remembering things.

Active recall is definitely effective for theoretical subjects. I should try using that more for my literature class. But for math, nothing beats just grinding through problems. Also, don't forget to, like, schedule in breaks. It's so easy to burn out if you're just studying non-stop. I try to do 50 minutes on, 10 minutes off.

Yeah, breaks are super important. I've also been thinking about starting a study group for the economics module. Sometimes explaining concepts to someone else helps me understand them better, and they can catch things I've missed. Plus, it breaks up the boringness of studying alone, which can get really isolating.

Study groups can be, like, tricky, though. I've been in groups where we spent more time chatting than actually studying, or someone just wants answers handed to them. You have to be really strict with yourselves about it. I prefer studying alone and then just checking in with friends for specific questions.

That's true, you need the right people and, like, a clear plan. We'd definitely need to set some rules, like focusing on specific chapters or problem sets. I think the key is to use it for reviewing difficult topics or quizzing each other, not for initial learning. It's also about keeping each other on track.

Beyond all the study techniques, I think it's just as important to look after yourself. I know it sounds a bit old-fashioned to say, but getting enough sleep and eating properly makes a huge difference in how much information you can actually remember. Pulling all-nighters just isn't good for the long term; you end up forgetting everything the next day anyway.

Totally agree, Lily. I made that mistake in my first year and really regretted it. Now, I make sure to shut down my laptop an hour before bed and do something relaxing, like reading. It helps clear my head. It's all about finding that balance between studying really hard and not burning out completely.

title: Improve Skills in Presentation 增强演讲技能
discussion_text:
Three teachers are discussing how to improve skills in presentation.

Hey guys, I'm really struggling with my upcoming presentation. I just don't know how to get better at this. Every time I stand up there, my mind goes blank.

Oh, I know how that feels. Honestly, the best thing that worked for me was just tons of practice. Why don't you practice in front of me? I can just sit and listen, and then give you some honest feedback afterwards.

Yeah, practice is huge. It really does make you feel more confident once you've run through it a dozen times. What's the specific part that trips you up, Ben?

Thanks, Claire, that would be awesome. For me, David, it's that I totally rely on my notes. If I don't have them, I'm convinced I'll miss a whole section of information and look like a fool.

See, that's exactly what we can work on. Maybe in the first few run-throughs, you use your notes, and then slowly try to wean off them.

I have a trick for that. About the nerves and eye contact... instead of looking directly into people's eyes, which can be super intense, try just looking at their chin or forehead. Or look at a pencil on someone's table. It looks like you're making eye contact, but it's way less stressful.

Their chin? Really? I've never heard that before. Doesn't it look weird?

Not at all! From a few feet away, no one can tell the difference. It totally works. It helps you feel like you're not under a microscope.

That's a great tip. So, how about this, Ben? You practice your presentation using David's trick, and I'll be your test audience. Afterward, I can tell you if your delivery seemed natural and which parts you might not need notes for.

Yeah, okay. That actually sounds like a solid plan. Practice to build confidence, a friendly face for feedback, and a new trick to handle the eye contact pressure. I already feel a bit better about this. Thanks, you two.

title: The New Library 新图书馆
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the new library at their university. 

Have you guys seen the new library on campus yet? It’s absolutely stunning, right? I went there yesterday afternoon to check it out, and I was really impressed. The whole front of the building is a huge glass wall, which lets in lots of soft, natural light. It’s way better than the old one.

Oh, I know! I’ve been looking forward to its opening for months. I was so excited when I heard it finally opened last week. But honestly, I went there to study this morning and found it’s really noisy inside. Students are always talking loudly in the hallways, and some even use laptops with loud keyboards. I might still choose to study at home.

The new library is really nice, but I have a small complaint too—the meeting rooms are just too big, making it hard to have a quiet discussion. I really wish they had added more small meeting rooms, maybe for 3 to 5 people, so we can work on group projects or have discussions more comfortably.

Yeah, speaking of complaints, I’ve noticed it’s been really crowded these days. All the reading seats are taken, and there aren’t any computers available if you arrive later than 10 am. But I think that’s just because it’s newly opened—everyone is curious and wants to check it out.

You’re probably right about that. After all, the new library is still way better than the old one. The chairs in the old library were all worn out and really uncomfortable to sit on, while the new chairs are soft and have adjustable backs.

Well, the other thing that bothers me a little is the artwork at the entrance. It’s really weird—I can’t even tell what it’s supposed to be. But other than that, everything else is perfect: clean, bright, and well-equipped. 

Really? I actually quite like that artwork! I think it’s pretty unique and creative. It adds a fun, modern touch to the library. I know it’s a bit strange, but maybe you just need to look at it a little longer to appreciate it. Overall, I’m really happy with the new library.

title: A Trip to Iceland 冰岛之旅
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing their upcoming trip to Iceland.

Speaker 1 (Male)
I’m really delighted about our trip to Iceland. There are so many things I want to see, especially the volcanoes and the beautiful beaches nearby. We’re also going to visit a national park where you can actually see where two continents connect. But I think diving is probably the activity I’m looking forward to the most.

Speaker 2 (Female)
I’m really happy with the activities we’ve planned as well. The volcano scenery should be amazing, and I’d definitely like to spend some time at the beach. I like diving too, although sometimes the water can be too cold for me. Personally, I think Iceland would be even better in winter because I really like hot springs. There are lots of natural hot springs there, so that’s something I’d really like to experience.

Speaker 3 (Male)
I’m really looking forward to the trip too. I’ve been to both Europe and North America before, but Iceland sounds completely different and amazing. I’m especially interested in the natural landscape and the black sun phenomenon. I think it’ll be great just to walk around the campsite and enjoy the nature around us.

Speaker 1 (Male)
There are some other unusual places we can visit as well. Apparently, there’s a road where you can drive under the cliffs and enjoy the scenery along the way. And apart from the volcanoes, there are natural hot springs in several areas. I think we’ll have plenty of opportunities to walk around and enjoy nature.

Speaker 2 (Female)
I also heard about some interesting swimming pools there. They’re actually former industrial sites, but now they look as if they were naturally formed. That sounds really interesting to me, especially because I enjoy swimming and hot springs. It could be nice to relax there after spending the day outdoors.

Speaker 3 (Male)
Yeah, I think we’ll have a good mix of activities on this trip. We can see the volcanoes and beaches, visit the national park, and spend some time walking around the campsite. We just need to make sure we follow the schedule because we’re returning on Friday afternoon. I’m sure it’s going to be an amazing trip.

Three students are discussing what to have for lunch after study.

Even though the food in the school cafeteria isn’t great, after all, they make really good coffee, which is exactly what I need right now.

title: Student Accommodation Choices 学生住宿选择
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the advantages and disadvantages of living on campus or off campus.

I’ve been living off campus for about a year now, and honestly I really enjoy it. It gives me a lot more freedom and convenience because I can organize my own schedule and lifestyle. But when you live with other people, you really need to set some rules in advance, especially about keeping the place clean and tidy. Otherwise, small problems can become very frustrating.

That makes sense. I still live in the dormitory with a lot of other students. One problem is that people sometimes use the toaster carelessly and set off the fire alarm. It’s happened several times this semester already. We all have to leave the building and stand outside very early in the morning, sometimes at five o’clock. It’s always freezing and everyone is half asleep.

Yeah, I’ve experienced that too. It’s definitely annoying, especially during winter. But overall, I still think living on campus is worth it. The rooms are fairly spacious, the price is cheaper than renting outside, and there are dormitory rules, so people usually live together quite peacefully.

I can understand that. The biggest downside for me is probably transportation. Since I live farther away from the university, I have to take the bus every day. Sometimes traffic is terrible, and getting to morning classes can be stressful.

That’s actually one of the reasons I prefer dorm life. I can walk to the classroom building in about two minutes, which saves a lot of time and energy. It’s especially convenient during exam periods when I spend most of the day on campus anyway.

I agree. I think both options have advantages and disadvantages. Living off campus gives you more independence, while dorm life is more convenient and affordable. It probably just depends on what kind of lifestyle you prefer.

title: Student Clubs 学生俱乐部
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing whether to join student clubs next semester.

Hey, have you guys thought about which clubs to join next term? I'm considering signing up for a couple-maybe the debate team and the photography society. I really want to meet people outside my major. Last year, joining the hiking club was amazing. I made so many friends during weekend trips!

Actually, I've decided not to join any clubs this year. I was part of the dance club last semester, and it took up way too much time. Rehearsals were twice a week, often until late, and it started affecting my grades. I'd rather focus on my studies and maybe pick up a part-time job instead.

I'm definitely joining at least one club! For me, it's not just about socializing—it's about building skills. I was in the robotics club last year, and I learned so much about project management and teamwork. Plus, it looks great on my CV.

That's a good point. I also think clubs help you develop soft skills, like how to communicate better and work in a group. And it's not all serious; sometimes it's just fun. Like in the hiking club, we ended up telling stories around campfires. Those were my best memories from last year.

I get that, but I often find club activities repetitive and poorly organized. A lot of time was wasted in meetings that could've been emails. I'd rather use that time to relax alone or hang out with a few close friends.

I see what you mean, but I've had the opposite experience. The robotics club was super well-run, and we even got to compete nationally. It gave me a real sense of achievement. I don't think I would've had that opportunity if I hadn't joined.

Exactly! It's all about finding the right club. I guess it depends on your interests and how the club is managed. But for me, the social and personal growth aspects are totally worth the time. It's really helped me become more confident and outgoing in general. Plus, being part of a community makes campus feel smaller and more like home.

Well, I'm happy with my decision to sit this one out. I prefer having control over my schedule. Last year, I always felt rushed trying to balance club events with assignments. Sometimes saying "no" is the best way to protect your mental health and academic goals. Knowing your limits is just as important as pushing your boundaries.

That's fair. But for anyone looking to gain more than just academic knowledge, I'd really recommend giving clubs a try. You might be surprised by what you can learn outside the classroom. Even just attending a few meetings can open doors to new interests and connections you never expected. It's not just about padding your resume-it's about discovering what you're truly passionate about.

discussion_text:

Well, I actually quite like group discussions. I will have a chance to learn from my peers, hear new ways of thinking, and sometimes even get help from partners when there is a problem. The group discussion can make the whole learning process more collaborative and less stressful.

I totally get what you mean about helping each other—that’s really valuable. I think it’s fine to discuss ideas and share perspectives. But I’m not comfortable actually creating the work as a group, because when too many people try to write or build something together, it often becomes messy or unproductive—no one’s voice comes through clearly, and it can even lead to disagreements.

Agreed! Finding the right partners and dividing group tasks properly can be quite challenging, yet it’s essential for a productive group discussion. Poor coordination in these areas often leads to misunderstandings or even conflict.

title: AI Proofreading 人工智能校对
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing using AI for proofreading.

Hey guys, have you ever thought about using AI for proofreading? I just got feedback on my essay from my tutor, and she said I need to proofread it. I’m wondering if I can use AI for things like grammar checks or even getting new ideas. 

That's an interesting point, but there is a significant risk of being accused of plagiarism if you use AI. Many universities are now implementing strict policies about AI-generated content. If the AI suggests substantial changes to your sentence structures or replaces too many of your original words, the final work might not truly be yours anymore. 

Well, I don’t mind using AI as long as it’s for educational purposes and used responsibly. After all, students often use computer software to check grammar, and we’re expected to learn from others’ words to build our own vocabulary. In the past, we used dictionaries to check grammar—it’s really no different from using AI.

Well, I get your point. I think the line when it comes to using AI for proofreading can get really blurry. I definitely don’t want to be suspected of plagiarism, so is there another way I can improve my assignments next time without using AI?

I’m not sure. I still think this needs to be considered carefully. For example, when Word marks mistakes with red and green underlines, is that considered AI-assisted proofreading? Different institutions and even different professors may have different standards for what counts as acceptable AI use. I’d be especially careful with major assignments or final papers.

Actually, I've already been using AI on my tablet for proofreading for a while now. But, I still get asked by my teacher to do another proofread myself. I think the key thing is, you won't get any new ideas from AI. AI will only make your existing ideas clearer and more correct. It's really just an advanced tool that helps polish your work, not something that creates content for you. The fundamental thinking and ideas still need to come from you.

Okay, I see. Thanks. I think I'll go back and ask for advice from my tutor about it first. I really don't want to be accused of plagiarism, especially since I'm not clear on where the line is drawn. It's better to be safe and get proper guidance rather than risk any academic consequences.

title: How to Manage Assignments 如何规划作业

Exactly! Why don’t we just do the next assignment together? That way, we can plan together, keep each other motivated, and also practice as a group.

title: Bookstore Closed 书店关门
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing the recent closure of their university bookstore.

I was really sad to hear that our university bookstore closed. I guess it’s because e-books are seen as better than physical books these days. Honestly, I do find e-books super convenient—you can carry hundreds of them on your phone and read anywhere—but my eyes get tired easily after long reading sessions.

Yeah, it’s such a shame. I really enjoyed the bookstore. Maybe most students feel the same way you do, so physical books are losing their place. But I’m firmly on Team Physical! I can easily highlight key points or jot down notes in the margins, and e-books just don’t give me that same sense of focus. You know, what saddens me the most is that the staff were always so kind—they’d quickly help you find textbooks and even recommend useful reference books.发言人2（男）

I see both of your points! E-books are great for on-the-go studying, but physical books are definitely better for deep reading. But I have to say that e-books would be more suitable for the current life and reading habits of students. And you’re absolutely right about the staff—they were so approachable. I once forgot my wallet there, and they kept it safe for me until I came back. Also, I think the bookstore could have avoided closing if it had adapted earlier—like by selling phone chargers, notebooks, pens, or other stationery. Students always need those items, and that could have brought in more customers.

Exactly! Stationery and tech accessories are daily necessities for us. The bookstore used to sell only books, which was too narrow a focus. If they’d added practical items—like folders, sticky notes, or other school supplies—more students would’ve stopped by regularly. It’s sad to lose such a friendly spot, but it’s a good lesson: adapting to what students actually need is key.

For sure! Whether we prefer e-books or physical books, having a campus store that offers a variety of useful items would be incredibly convenient. It’s not just about books anymore; it’s about creating a one-stop spot that supports students’ everyday academic life.

title: Course to Take Next Semester 下学期选课
discussion_text:
Three speakers are discussing which course to take next semester.

So, have you guys checked out the course list for next semester? I skimmed through it, and I think we should pick something that’s actually helpful for our major. It’ll make the whole learning experience way more meaningful and engaging.

Absolutely! I was thinking the exact same thing. There’s no point taking a class just because it’s easy or gives out high grades if it doesn’t actually help us in our field. I think we should go for a course that builds real, practical skills—even if it’s challenging. You’ll be curious and want to dig deeper and will get so much more out of it in the long run.

Honestly, I think the most important thing is to choose a course you’re interested in—even if it’s not directly related to your major. I’m a business student, but I’ve always been fascinated by languages and different cultures. That’s why I’m signing up for Spanish next semester.

I agree that how interesting a course really is matters. But, if this course is only interesting yet not helpful for your major, it's somewhat like a waste of time. After all, we should focus on the input-output benefits and whether it will be helpful for future job hunting. Plus, we also need to consider the course’s difficulty level—after all, passing the final exam should be a realistic goal.

I actually disagree with the idea that Spanish isn’t useful for business—it’s the opposite! Honestly, I think language courses are valuable no matter what you study because being able to speak another language is a huge advantage in today’s global market. Whether you’re negotiating with international clients, working on a multicultural team, or even just traveling for work, communication skills go a long way.

Actually, I didn't think that much. I am really just interested in Spanish. I think when you’re genuinely interested in the subject, you’re way more likely to pay attention and put in your effort. And let’s be honest—even if the class is tough, that motivation can at least help you pass.

title: Joining or Starting a Club 参加还是创建社团
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing which student club to join next semester.

Hey, I’ve been thinking about joining a club next semester, but I’m not really sure which one to choose. Do you guys have any suggestions on what I should join? I want something interesting, but also something that’s actually worth my time.

Honestly, I think it really depends on your interests. You should choose something you genuinely enjoy, otherwise it’s hard to stay committed. And you know, if you can’t find a club that fits you, you could even start your own club. That way, you can shape it exactly the way you want.

Start my own club? That sounds a bit challenging. I’ve never really thought about that before.

Actually, I joined the debate club last year, and it’s been a great experience. But I have to say, running a club—or even being actively involved—does require quite a lot of organization. There are usually different roles, like a president, a vice president, event coordinators, and people responsible for promotion and logistics. Everyone has their own responsibilities to keep things running smoothly.

Exactly. That’s why starting your own club can be rewarding, but it also comes with a lot of responsibility. You need people to manage different aspects, and it takes time to build everything from scratch.

Yeah, in the debate club, we also have regular training sessions, internal competitions, and even external tournaments. Some people focus on preparing arguments, while others help organize events or manage the team. It’s quite structured, and that’s why it works so well.

Hmm, hearing all that, I think starting my own club might be too much for me. I’m not really prepared to take on that kind of responsibility. I guess I’d rather just join an existing club instead of creating one from scratch.

That’s totally fine. Joining an established club is definitely easier, and you can still gain a lot from it without the pressure of managing everything.

Yeah, and you can always try a few different clubs at the beginning of the semester. Most clubs have trial sessions, so you can see what suits you best before committing.

That sounds like a good plan. I’ll probably start by exploring a few options and then decide from there.

title: Department's 10th Anniversary Party 庆祝部门十周年
discussion_text:
Three teachers are discussing how to celebrate the Department's 10th Anniversary party.

For our department's 10th anniversary, I think we should book that Greek restaurant downtown. It has excellent reviews, and the atmosphere would be perfect for a special celebration. We deserve something memorable after a decade of hard work!

I understand the appeal, but that restaurant is quite expensive, and it's far from campus. Many colleagues might find it inconvenient to travel there after work. Why don't we host it on campus instead? It would be more budget-friendly and accessible for everyone.

Not the Mathematics Building restaurant, though—the space is too cramped, and the decor is so dull. It wouldn’t feel like a proper celebration there.

What about the Business Building’s private event room? It’s spacious, recently renovated, and we can arrange catering. It’s a good compromise—still on campus but more upscale than our department’s facilities.

That’s a practical suggestion. Now, how many people should we invite? Initially, I thought just faculty members, but with only 15 of us, it might feel too small.

We could include some of our first graduating students! They were part of our department’s early years, and it would be meaningful to have them join.

Agreed. A mix of current faculty and selected alumni would make it more special. Let’s finalize the Business Building as the venue and start compiling the guest list.

title: Revising the First Essay 修改第一篇论文

A tutor and two students are discussing how to revise their first essay.

It’s fine. You don’t need to worry too much about the word count this time. After all, this is your first time writing this kind of essay. But you should avoid giving too many details. Try to focus on the key points. Also, don’t repeat the same words too often in many paragraphs. Too much repetition can make your writing sound weak.

Actually, I repeat words deliberately because they are very important. I thought that, in that case, it could represent our main points more clearly.

I understand why you did that, but that’s not the best way to show your main points. Instead of repeating the same words, you can use clear topic sentences and stronger explanations. That will make your argument easier to follow.

So we should write the key points more clearly. And we should reduce repeating words.

Exactly. Just check your essay again and confirm that your main ideas are clear. Then you can submit it.

Thank you. That makes me feel more confident about revising it.

You’re welcome. Don’t worry too much, and good luck with your submission.

title: Using Mobile Phones in Lectures 课堂上用手机
discussion_text:
Three tutors are discussing the use of mobile phones in lectures.

Okay team, let's talk about something that's been bothering me. What do you think of students using mobile phones in lectures? Honestly, it drives me crazy.

Well, actually, I feel okay with students using a mobile phone in my class. Firstly, some students use their phone to record the lecture, which can be really helpful for reviewing later. Secondly, we have many international students whose English isn't perfect; they often need to quickly check words or translations during the lecture to keep up.

I know, I get what you're saying, but in my experience, they always seem to get distracted and start chatting with friends on their phones instead of paying attention. You never really know what they're actually doing on there.

I see both sides, but I think it's not necessary to put a full ban on mobile phones in lectures. Sometimes, I will even ask my students to use their phones for in-class activities, like polls or quick research, to make the lesson more interactive.

That's a good point. Maybe we could have a meeting—a lunch meeting on Tuesday, perhaps—to discuss this further and share best practices?

Yes, I agree. This is a broader issue. We should also bring this idea to the next department conference and try to think of a clear, fair policy with the whole department.

title: Free Online Courses 免费在线课程
discussion_text:
Three teachers are discussing free online courses.

Actually, I've been looking into the growth of free online courses lately and found that there are now many free online courses. It's impressive how many well-known universities offer free online courses nowadays.

Yes! I think it is too good to be true. What about you? Do you think the free online courses offer benefits to students?

Exactly! I think it's a very good idea, especially when you consider accessibility. Many people simply cannot attend traditional school because of their financial situation, so these courses can be a real benefit to those learners. But you know what, I've noticed a real gap between offering and uptake. Many students just do not take part.

That’s true. Because many students do not have time to take these free online courses. I suggest universities could reschedule these courses to other times to attract more outsiders to join.

And you know what, I can hardly believe so few people who enroll see it through to the end.

Yes, that happens a lot. Actually, those who have the desire to study are often the most likely to complete the courses. Some people are discouraged by the tedious coursework, as they discover that a large amount of work is required. Another reason for the low completion is that these courses are free, so students don’t face any financial punishment.

title: How to Plan an Essay 如何写好论文
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing how to plan an essay.

Guys, I’m really struggling with this essay. It’s so much more difficult than I expected, and I don’t even know where to begin. I usually start by drafting the conclusion, but that would be a disaster if I’ve misinterpreted the question right from the beginning.

Hey, don’t worry too much about it. The first thing you should do is make sure you understand the question. Read it carefully and figure out exactly what it’s asking. Then, plan your essay with a clear idea of what you’re supposed to discuss.

Oh, so you all do the reading first and then the planning? I do the exact opposite! I start by outlining my essay’s structure first, and then go back to carefully read the question and relevant materials. I find that this way, I have a clearer idea of what kind of information I need to look for and use.

Well, I think the order really doesn’t matter at all. Both reading and planning are really important—but honestly, what’s even more valuable is getting someone else to read your work. What you really need is their feedback: fresh eyes can spot things you’ve missed, and their suggestions often help you see your essay in a whole new light.

Well, I have to say that’s a good point. But it’s not easy to find someone else to read your essay. If you ask a classmate, you have to worry about whether they might copy your work, either consciously or unconsciously, ending up with similar ideas or content. Plus, you also need to consider whether they even have the time. I mean, our lecturers and tutors are always busy with their own classes and projects. And if you seek feedback from fellow students, I’m not sure they can give you truly meaningful or constructive comments.

Well, I think it’s a good idea to have someone read your essay and give feedback before you submit it. Don’t overthink finding the “perfect” person—after all, I’m sure I can find at least one person who’s willing and able to help. And once I get their suggestions, I can always decide whether or not to take them after thinking things through carefully. Honestly, that sounds like a solid plan. I’m already feeling better about this essay!

Three students are discussing the advantages and disadvantages of studying in the library.

title: Complaint in the Library 图书馆投诉
discussion_text:
Two students are complaining to the library staff about the noise in the library.

Excuse me, I’d like to complain about the noise in the library. Some people treat this place like a club instead of a study area. The library is supposed to be a quiet place for people to study, but there are always people chatting and watching videos here without putting their headphones on.

Well, I'm aware of the situation you’ve complained about, but students’ behavior is difficult to manage because the library is really big and there are only a few staff around. It’s hard for us to monitor everything. You know, the library does have a silent zone, so if you’re distracted by noise here, you can call security and they’ll help resolve the problem. But we can’t control the noise from other areas, like the computer section. Talking is allowed outside the silent zones.

Well, in this case, may I offer you some suggestions? Why is it that people are required to keep quiet in the silent area, but talking isn't prohibited in the computer room? It seems a bit unfair to students who want to focus on studying, since the noise from the computer area can still be clearly heard and easily disturbs people nearby.

You'd better write down your complaints and suggestions, because the university takes advice from students seriously. By writing down your experience clearly, the school can better understand the noise problems in the library and take more effective measures to improve the study environment for everyone.

I also have something to complain about. I mean — can we bring food into the library? I often see students bringing all kinds of food to the study rooms and eating while they study. For example, some people bring strong-smelling food like instant noodles or takeout meals. These smells spread quickly in the library and make it really hard to concentrate. This is another big problem that influences our study environment.

Food from outside is not allowed in the library. Even food without strong smells, like bread, is not permitted. The movements and sounds people make while eating can really disturb others who are studying. We’ve been strictly enforcing this rule, but some students still break it. If you’re bothered by this again next time, you can ask security for help.

title: Where to Live in Final Year 最后一年住哪里
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing where to live in their final year.

So, have you guys thought about where to live for our final year?

Yeah, we’re planning to live off campus.

Oh, really? Why is that? I feel the opposite—I’m actually planning to move back into the school residence.

I get that. Living on campus is definitely nice—there are good facilities, entertainment, and plenty of support. Especially in the first year, I really needed that. But after two years, I feel like I want a change, so I’ve decided to go for a flat share.

Exactly. I also want a new environment and the chance to meet more people. And honestly, when it comes to exam season, I don’t want to be in the library surrounded by stressed-out students, all fighting for a quiet spot.

That makes sense, but you do need to be careful when choosing who to live with. In my last two years, I was in a flat share, and my roommate only wanted to party instead of study. I ended up having to shut myself in my room just to get any work done.

That won’t be a problem for me. Four of us—close friends—have already decided to share a flat together. We’re all really ambitious, we can study together and stay focused, and honestly, we usually manage to get top grades anyway.

Same here. I already have a friend renting a place off campus, and he’s invited me to join him. We’ve known each other for years, we get along really well, and we’ve even agreed to keep the place tidy by sharing cleaning duties.

Oh, that’s smart. Cleaning is such a big issue. My old roommates never did any cleaning at all, and in the end it all fell on me.

title: Street Graffiti and Public Art 街头涂鸦与公共艺术
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing graffiti and street art.

Speaker 1 (Male)
When I was walking towards the train station yesterday, I passed an old factory wall covered with graffiti. I just stood there looking at it, and honestly, it was amazing. The paintings were so detailed and colorful that it almost felt like an outdoor art gallery.

Speaker 2 (Female)
Yes, but isn’t it illegal? Even if it isn’t, I think it probably should be. Personally, I’m against it because it’s basically vandalism. A lot of people do it during the night when there are no police around, and usually they even have someone watching out for them.

Speaker 3 (Female)
I agree to some extent. There are other places where they can paint and express themselves, and nowadays there are also online platforms. Artists can post their work on the Internet instead of painting on public walls.

Speaker 1 (Male)
But I wasn’t talking about random writing or tagging. I mean actual paintings of people on the street, wearing sunglasses and things like that. Some of them are incredibly creative. I stood there for quite a while just looking at them and thinking. It made the whole area feel more alive and interesting.

Speaker 2 (Female)
I understand what you mean, but surely there should be designated places for that kind of art. Artists could also sell their work online or display it legally in galleries instead of painting on factory walls without permission.

Speaker 3 (Female)
Personally, I don’t like the idea of doing absolutely everything online. Seeing artwork in real public spaces feels different. It creates an atmosphere that you can’t really experience through a screen.

Speaker 1 (Male)
Exactly. I think artists should have some freedom to express themselves in public spaces, especially when the artwork actually improves the environment instead of damaging it.

Speaker 2 (Female)
Maybe. But I still think there should be rules and designated areas. I actually know an artist who paints legally in public spaces, and his work is still very popular without causing problems for anyone.

title: Project Meeting Place 项目会议地点
discussion_text:
Three students are discussing their project meeting place on campus.

I think we should meet in a conference room in the university library. We can conveniently borrow books we need right there while we work. It's a quiet space with plenty of resources, and we won't have to carry heavy books around later. Plus, the library has those small study rooms we can book if we need complete privacy.

I'm not so sure about that idea the library is always so crowded during this time of day. There will be too many people studying and chatting outside the rooms, and it will be very noisy even inside the conference areas. Last time I tried to study there, I could hardly concentrate with all the distractions. Maybe we should consider someplace else that's actually quiet.

I have a compromise-we can go to the library first to borrow all the books we need for our research in the morning. Then, we can catch up online. This way we get a quiet space to discuss in our own home.

I totally agree! In this way, we can search for resources online at any time! Let’s find a coffee shop to sit down and make a perfect task plan! Which coffee shop were you thinking about? There are several near campus, but most tend to be quite busy. Maybe we should look for someplace less popular?

I like the idea, but I have to go back home around 4 PM to receive a package that's being delivered. I don't want to miss it, so it might make me a little late for the meeting. How about we meet at the coffee shop near the city center?

No, not that one. There are so many people and it’s too crowded. What about that new place called "Sweet Treats"? It's a bit farther from campus, but I heard they have nice cakes and coffee. When you arrive, just find the long table on the first floor. We’ll be there waiting for you.

OK! Let’s pick this one! I've passed by Sweet Treats a few times it does look cozy because it usually has fewer people. Plus, who can say no to sweet treats while working, right? Oh, and just remember to call us when you go out of home so we know when to expect you. We can start without you and fill you in when you arrive. If anything urgent comes up, we can always hop on a quick online call to keep you in the loop.

Great, then it's settled! We'll meet at the library at 3 PM, get our books, then walk over to Sweet Treats to assign tasks and discuss the project outline. Don't forget to call us when you're on your way!
